title: Online exam
like: a timed online exam for 200,000 students
brief: A national board runs a two-hour online exam for 200,000 students in three regions at the same time. Answers save automatically every half minute, a live heartbeat shows the student is still there, and proctoring marks suspicious events. Every saved answer matters. A minute of outage at the wrong time is a national story.

clarify.q: Can the exam start late for everyone?
clarify.a: Yes, if it must. But students already inside cannot lose answers or time.

clarify.q: How often does a student's browser talk to us?
clarify.a: An autosave about every 30 seconds and a heartbeat about every 20 seconds, so the load is steady and large.

clarify.q: Is the sign-in rush at the start?
clarify.a: Yes. Most students sign in within a few minutes before 9 am, about three times the normal level.

clarify.q: What does an expired certificate do?
clarify.a: Browsers refuse to connect at all. Everyone is locked out until someone finds and replaces it.

notes: Load is nearly flat during the exam window and falls to almost nothing after.
Heartbeats are small and can be lost; saved answers cannot.

numbers.label: Open connections
numbers.how: one per student, about 2 gateway nodes per 200k at 100k each, approx.

hints: Every student is far from at least one region. A global load balancer sends each to the nearest healthy one.
Saved answers must not be lost, so use a store that spans zones with synchronous copies; heartbeats can go to a fast key-value store.
Cutoff, final submission and autosave ordering must have one authoritative policy. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: The traffic is a steady, large, write-heavy stream from three continents. Put a front in each region, keep answers in a replicated store, and make a silent failure loud: a certificate or a bad push should page someone within a minute.

designs.name: Three fronts, one safe answer store
designs.why: A global load balancer sends each student to a regional front. Each front runs its own servers; heartbeats go to a key-value store and answers to a distributed SQL database spread over three zones. A synthetic probe, alerting and a pager catch a certificate failure fast, and a secrets and config service lets the team replace it.

tradeoffs: A key-value store for heartbeats is cheap and fast; sending heartbeats to the answer database would triple its cost for data nobody keeps.
A global store spanning regions adds round-trip time for far-away students, so answers are saved in the nearest copy and replicated; a lost region costs a few seconds of replay, not an exam.
A probe and a pager add little to the bill and cut the detection of a silent failure from 15 or more minutes to about one.
Overprovisioning for the start rush is cheap for two hours and wasteful for the other 22; autoscale and short pre-warming keep the average low.
editorial.realWorld: Large remote exams have been taken by hundreds of thousands at once; the typical failure was not capacity but a shared dependency such as identity, a certificate or a single region (approx.). A synthetic check that logs in every minute catches many of those.

correctness.prompt: Online exam: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Recover versioned saved answers without accepting stale autosaves or ambiguous cutoff. Transport order cannot define the latest answer. The visible saved state must correspond to a durable acknowledgement. Cutoff, final submission and autosave ordering must have one authoritative policy.

fields.label: Step 1. Autosave version 12 arrives before delayed version 11. What is retained?
options: 12, with a conditional version check and durable receipt
fields.explanation: Transport order cannot define the latest answer.

fields.label: Step 2. The save reply is lost just before a regional outage. What can a student trust?
options: The green UI indicator before server acknowledgement
A durable save receipt under the declared recovery boundary, with retryable edit ids
fields.explanation: The visible saved state must correspond to a durable acknowledgement.

fields.label: Step 3. The exam ends while an autosave is in flight. What governs acceptance?
options: An explicit server cutoff policy and recoverable final submission state
Whichever browser clock says the student finished
fields.explanation: Cutoff, final submission and autosave ordering must have one authoritative policy.

correctness.responsibility: Recover versioned saved answers without accepting stale autosaves or ambiguous cutoff.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
